input:
Als ich im August 2019 zum ersten Mal die Werkstatt in der Mainzer Straße betrat, wusste ich noch nicht, dass dieser Ort mein Leben verändern würde. Mein Onkel Peter hatte dort ein kleines Reparaturgeschäft für Fahrräder und Motorroller, und ich verbrachte jeden Nachmittag zwischen Ölkannen und Werkzeugkisten. Eines Tages brachte eine Kundin einen alten Golf mit dem Kennzeichen HH-AB 1408, der seit Wochen nicht mehr anspringen wollte. Ich durfte die Elektronik prüfen, und nach drei Stunden Fehlersuche fanden wir ein durchgescheuertes Kabel am Zündschloss. Dieses Erfolgserlebnis hat mich mehr geprägt als jede Note in der Schule.

Seitdem dokumentiere ich meine Projekte auf meinem Kanal unter dem Namen @pascal_schraubt, wo ich Schritt für Schritt zeige, wie man Fehler systematisch eingrenzt. Die Resonanz hat mich überrascht: Zuschauer aus Leipzig, Bremen und sogar aus Wien schreiben mir, wenn sie selbst an einem Problem hängen. Peter sagt immer, dass gute Mechanik mit Geduld beginnt, nicht mit Werkzeug. Dieser Satz begleitet mich bis heute.

Ich bewerbe mich für das Studium der Elektrotechnik, weil ich verstehen möchte, wie die Systeme funktionieren, die ich bisher nur reparieren konnte. Ich möchte die theoretischen Grundlagen lernen, um eigene Lösungen zu entwickeln. Am 14. August 2024 werde ich volljährig, und ich freue mich darauf, diesen neuen Abschnitt mit einer klaren Richtung zu beginnen.

Dear Journal,

I keep telling myself that the panic attacks are getting less frequent, but last Thursday on the Rue des Martyrs I had to stand against a shop window for twenty minutes before I could breathe properly. Amélie from the office found me, sat down on the kerb beside me without asking questions, and walked me back to my flat in the Marais. She said I should write things down, so here I am. Dr. Fontaine wants me to track the triggers: crowds, the metro at rush hour, unanswered emails. My registration for the Peugeot is AB-214-QK if I need to remember where I parked, and my client portal login is alexandra.moreau@lumiere-conseil.fr, which I check far too often.

Session went well on the 4th of December. Dr. Fontaine asked me to name one thing I did for myself that week, and I said I had bought a proper notebook, which made her smile. We talked about my national ID, 13 66 04 92 817 00, which I had to dig out for the bank and which made me feel oddly exposed, as if my whole life were a file. I am trying to notice that feeling instead of obeying it.

Amélie has invited me to the Canal Saint-Martin on Sunday, and I think I will go, even if I leave early. Writing this has helped more than I expected. Tomorrow I will try to write one thing I am grateful for, even a small one. The bread from the corner bakery counts.

A.

input: I am a systems engineer who has spent most of my career building reliable infrastructure for small teams that cannot afford downtime. My work focuses on observability, incident response and making complex distributed systems easier to reason about. Outside the office I mentor junior developers, contribute to open-source tooling and spend too many weekends experimenting with home automation. input:
Dear Grandma Ruth,

I hope this letter finds you well and that the cold in Ohio isn't bothering your knees too much. I think about you every time I pass the kitchen and smell cinnamon, which is just what I'd expect from you. Mom says you've been busy with the church bake sale committee again, and I can only imagine how many pies that involved.

I wanted to tell you some news before Thanksgiving so you'd have time to brag about me to your friends at bingo. I finally got accepted into the nursing program at Riverside Memorial Hospital's training partnership, starting in January. Me, a nurse! I still remember you telling me I had steady hands when I helped you thread that needle for your quilt. Dad says I have to be at the orientation on November 14th, so I'm pretty nervous but mostly excited.

I also started a job at Brightwater Logistics last month, answering phones and helping with scheduling. My manager, Gary Lindqvist, is strict but fair, and the people there are kind. Mostly I'm writing because I'm turning 19 this year and I wanted you to know how much your advice has stuck with me. I still keep your note in my wallet. Please give Grandpa Walt a hug from me, and call when you have a minute so we can talk properly.

All my love,
Gracie

input:
After nine years at Harrowgate Logistics, I've made the decision to step into a new chapter. On Monday 12 May I start as Senior Operations Lead at Brightwater Freight in Newtown, and I wanted to share a bit about why.

When I joined Harrowgate at 27, I was a coordinator who loved spreadsheets and was honestly a bit scared of meetings. Nine years later I've led three regional rollouts, managed a team of fourteen, and learned more from the people on the dock than from any course. I'm grateful for every one of those years, and for the leaders who backed me when I made mistakes.

So why move? Mostly because I want to build something from the ground up again. Brightwater is growing fast across Sydney and into Newcastle, and the role gives me a chance to shape how a team scales rather than just keep the machine running. The conversations in the interview felt like a real partnership, and that matters to me more than a title.

I also know that change is hard for the people around you. If you're on my team at Harrowgate, thank you. I'll be keeping in touch, and I'm happy to talk through anything you're weighing up in your own career. Feel free to reach out at vanessa.drummond@harrowgate.com.au before I leave on 9 May.

If you've made a similar leap, I'd love to hear how it went for you. What did you wish you'd known before you started? Drop your advice in the comments. I'll be reading every one.

On to the next chapter, and thank you for being part of this one.

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Ramon, Dominic's college roommate, and I've been asked to say a few words about the man we all call Dodong. I still remember the first night we met in Naga, when he insisted on carrying my suitcase up four flights of stairs and then told me, with a straight face, that it was his way of saying welcome to Bicol. Nobody had ever tried so hard to make a stranger feel at home.

Dominic grew up in Naga City, and he has never let anyone forget it. He's the first to tell you about the best halo-halo in town and the last to leave a family gathering. Over the years I've watched him show up for friends with the same quiet loyalty. When my father was in the hospital last year, Dodong drove six hours from Manila on a Tuesday just to sit in the waiting room with me and bring pandesal for the nurses.

So to Dominic and Mariel, I raise my glass. Mariel, you've taken on a man who will fix your car, forget your birthday once, and then make it up to you with a surprise trip to Siargao on the fourteenth of October. Thank you for choosing him. Dodong, you finally got the girl and the happy ending. Cheers to the two of you.

She has started leaving dishes in the sink for days, and when I bring it up she laughs it off or says I'm overreacting. Last week I found out she had been using my savings card to pay for a few things and didn't tell me until I asked. I don't want to blow up the friendship, but I also feel like I've been quietly resentful for months and it's starting to affect how I feel when I walk through the door.

To whom it may concern,

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for Fiona Lavoie, who worked under my supervision as a senior accounts analyst at Brightwater Logistics in Halifax from March 2019 until her departure on April 12, 2024. I have managed finance teams for nearly twenty years, and in that time I have rarely worked with someone as thorough, dependable and quick to take initiative as Fiona.

Fiona joined our team after completing her Bachelor of Commerce at Dalhousie University, and she brought a sharp analytical mind to every project she touched. Within her first year she rebuilt our month-end reconciliation process, reducing the close cycle from nine working days to five. She did this without being asked, and she documented every change so that the rest of the department could follow it. Colleagues often came to her with questions that had nothing to do with her job description, and she answered them patiently and accurately.

What stood out most was her composure under pressure. During the audit season of 2022, when a vendor migration left us with significant discrepancies, Fiona worked late for three weeks straight. She kept the external auditors informed, explained every adjustment clearly, and never once let frustration show in her communication. Her steadiness gave the rest of the team confidence when we needed it most.

Outside the office, Fiona is a devoted member of her community. She volunteers every second Saturday at a food bank on Gottingen Street and serves as treasurer for her neighbourhood association. She lives at 418 Ravenscroft Crescent in Halifax with her partner and their dog, Biscuit, who has become something of a mascot in her building. Her colleagues have often joked that Fiona is the only person they know who can balance a spreadsheet and a dog walking schedule with equal precision.

I recommend Fiona Lavoie without reservation for any role in finance, operations or management. She is honest, capable and genuinely kind, and any organization fortunate enough to hire her will benefit quickly. Please feel free to contact me at fiona.recommend@brightwaterlogistics.ca or at 902-555-0147 should you require any further information.

Sincerely,

Marcus Doucette
Director of Finance, Brightwater Logistics

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Samuel Okonkwo-Bello, Chiamaka's older brother, and I've been asked to say a few words tonight. I'm told I have five minutes, which for a man who has known Chiamaka since she was a loud, bossy six-year-old is not nearly enough.

When Chiamaka was twelve she decided, without consulting anyone, that she would become a lawyer. She practised her closing arguments on our cousins during Christmas and on the gate man at 14 Adetokunbo Crescent, Lekki Phase 1, Lagos, every Saturday for two years. Our mother still says he was the only person in the family who never once asked her to stop. Tonight I want to thank Chiamaka's husband, Sola, who has been patient, funny and brave enough to argue with her and win occasionally. Sola, you have married a woman who will always have the last word, and you have chosen it perfectly.

Chiamaka, Chi-Chi, the girl I used to carry on my shoulders at Ibadan Market, you have made your family proud in more ways than I can list. Your Ogechi, who is now twenty-nine but still insists she is twenty-six, sends her love. On behalf of everyone here, may your marriage be long, your arguments short and your laughter louder than both. Please join me in raising your glasses to the bride and groom.

input:
June 14th. Athens is unbearably hot today, and I spent the whole afternoon at the ministry office in Syntagma trying to renew my residence paperwork. Orestis, the clerk behind the glass, was kind enough but insisted I bring my passport number written out in full, AB4471829, plus a photocopy of the ID card. I had both in my tote bag, folded in a plastic sleeve, and I still managed to forget the stamps. Turning thirty-four in a few weeks makes these bureaucratic errands feel even more absurd, as if the government thinks I can still pass for someone younger and more patient.

After the office I walked down to Plaka with Eleni, who has been my closest friend since we shared a flat in Thessaloniki. We ate grilled octopus under a vine and argued about whether Crete or the Cyclades will win the summer. She keeps teasing me that Orestis only looked at my papers because I smiled at him, and maybe she is right. Her phone buzzed twice during dinner, a reminder of the tasks waiting for us both.

On the bus home I kept thinking about how much of my life is now written down in numbers and files. Tomorrow I will go back with the stamps, and hopefully that will be the end of it. I want to write something real this summer, not just forms. Maybe that starts with this diary.

I have been going to Sharma Auto Care in Indiranagar for almost six years now, and I finally feel I should write something about them. My car is a 2014 Honda City, registration KA-03-MX-4417, and I have never once been made to feel like a number at this place. The workshop sits on a small lane just off 100 Feet Road, so parking is a bit tight, but the staff always wave you into a spot.

Last month my brake pads started squealing badly on the drive to the office. I called on a Tuesday morning and was told they could look at it that same afternoon. The service advisor, Rohan Kulkarni, who is the Service Manager at the workshop, walked me through the inspection report on a tablet, with photos of the worn pads and the scored disc. He did not push any extra work on me. He said the front discs were still within limits and only the pads needed replacing, and he showed me exactly why.

My wife, Meenakshi, had her own experience there in March when the AC stopped cooling. She says the technician, Imran, spent almost an hour tracing a small refrigerant leak and did not charge her for the diagnostic because the fault turned out to be a faulty compressor clutch under warranty. She still talks about it. Her cousin who lives near Koramangala has started bringing his Maruti there too, after hearing us talk about it at a family dinner.

The billing is transparent. Every invoice lists parts and labour separately, and they keep the old parts in a bag for you if you ask. Pricing is in line with or a little below what the authorised dealers charge, which is the main reason I keep coming back. I once got a bill wrong by a few hundred rupees and they corrected it within the hour without any argument.

The waiting area could use a better coffee machine and a few more chairs, but the Wi-Fi works and the tea is free. Appointments on weekdays are usually honoured, though Saturdays get crowded after about ten in the morning, so book ahead if you can.

Overall I would give Sharma Auto Care five stars without hesitation. Honest advice, fair prices and people who remember your name. If you live around Indiranagar or Domlur and need someone you can trust with your car, this is the place. I will be back in August for the scheduled service, and I expect nothing less.

input:
Growing up outside a small market town in the west of Ireland, I learned early that the most useful skills are the ones nobody writes on a timetable. On Saturday mornings I worked the counter at my family's shop, weighing vegetables, reckoning change in my head and listening to the regulars talk about weather, hurling and whatever had gone wrong in the village that week. Those mornings taught me more about patience and about people than any classroom ever did.

When I was fifteen I started volunteering with a local meals programme that ran out of a church hall twice a week. My job was mostly unglamorous: stacking chairs, sorting donated tins, pouring tea for people who came in from the cold. Over time I found myself drawn to the quieter tables, where older men sat alone and wanted someone to listen. I came to understand that a good conversation can be as nourishing as the food, and that dignity is something you can either protect or quietly erode with a careless word.

These experiences shaped the question that now drives my interest in social policy. Why do some communities hold together through hardship while others fray? input:
Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm Ricardo, and I've had the honour of being Vitor's best friend since we were nine years old, kicking a ball around the courtyard of our building in Tijuca. Back then I never imagined that the skinny kid who couldn't stop talking about football would one day stand here as the best man at his wedding. Life has a sense of humour.

When Vitor first told me he'd met Marina, he was sitting at our usual table at the bar on Rua Conde de Bonfim, and he had that look on his face, the one he gets when he's already decided something. He said, "Ricardo, I think this one is different." I rolled my eyes, of course. But then I met her, and I understood. She laughed at his terrible jokes, she argued with him about everything, and she somehow made him better without ever trying to change him. Their first date was supposed to be a quick coffee on March 14th. It turned into a six-hour conversation, and Vitor still insists that he paid, though I have witnesses who say otherwise.

So please raise your glasses with me. To Vitor and Marina, to the friendship that taught me what loyalty looks like, and to a love that started over a coffee and a bad joke. Saúde!

אני כותבת את זה בבוקר אחרי הפגישה עם נועם, כי אני יודעת שאם לא אכתוב עכשיו, אאבד את מה שהוא אמר. הוא שאל אותי מה השתנה מאז שחזרתי מהטיול בצפון, ולא ידעתי מה לענות. אמרתי שאני ישנה טוב יותר, וזה נכון, אבל לא סיפרתי לו על הלילות שאני מתעוררת ויושבת על קצה המיטה בלי סיבה.

אורית, החברה הכי טובה שלי מהאוניברסיטה, התקשרה אתמול בערב. היא רצתה לתאם את יום ההולדת שלה, ב-14 באוגוסט, והזמינה אותי לארוחה בתל אביב. שמחתי לשמוע את הקול שלה, אבל אחרי השיחה הרגשתי שאני מתרחקת ממנה. אני לא יודעת אם זה בגללי או בגללה, ואני מפחדת לשאול.

היום אני צריכה להביא לוועדה את המסמכים שלי לחידוש ההיתר לעבודה. בתיק כתוב מספר תעודת הזהות שלי, 034871569, ושם הדבר נראה כמו פרט טכני, אבל כשאני מסתכלת עליו אני נזכרת שכל הדברים שלי מסודרים במספרים ובתיקיות. נועם אמר שזה חלק ממה שאני מנסה לשלוט בו, ושאולי כדאי לדבר על זה יותר.

בפגישה דיברנו גם על אמא. היא ביקשה שנתראה ב-22 באוגוסט, בדיוק אחרי השבת, ואני עדיין לא החלטתי אם אני הולכת. בכל פעם שאני חושבת על זה, הגוף שלי מתכווץ. נועם שאל אם אני מרגישה שאני צריכה הגנה מהמפגש, ולהפתעתי עניתי שכן.

החלטתי לנסות משהו קטן השבוע: לכתוב לעצמי מכתב קצר בכל בוקר, בלי לערוך. אולי זה יעזור לי לראות את הדפוסים. אני לא בטוחה שזה יעבוד, אבל לפחות זו פעולה אחת שאני לוקחת בידיים שלי.

אני רוצה לזכור שהפגישה הזו הייתה מאומצת, ושבכל זאת יצאתי ממנה עם משהו. בפעם הבאה אני רוצה לדבר עם נועם על אורית, ועל למה אני מרגישה שאני צריכה לבחור בין להיות קרובה אליה לבין לשמור על עצמי.

Session notes, Thursday. Frankie came in looking tired but more open than last week. She said she has started going to Brightside Coffee on Ninth Street in the mornings instead of sitting at home with her laptop, and that the barista, a guy named Marcus, remembered her order after only two visits. She described it as small, but she said it was the first time in months she felt seen by someone who wasn't a family member. We talked about how much of her isolation has come from working remotely and telling herself she was fine.

We spent most of the hour on the anxiety she feels before calls with her sister, Jolene. Frankie admitted she rehearses every sentence in the car and then freezes once the phone rings. Hallo allemaal, ik hoop dat iemand me kan helpen. Ik ben Pieter van Dijk, 34 jaar, en ik woon al een paar jaar in Utrecht. Sinds begin maart heb ik last van een hardnekkige pijn in mijn onderrug die steeds erger wordt, vooral na het zitten op kantoor. Ik ben vorige week naar de huisarts gegaan in het Wilhelminapark, maar die zei alleen dat het waarschijnlijk spierpijn is en dat ik maar wat rust moet nemen. Ik heb het gevoel dat er meer aan de hand is, maar ik weet niet goed of ik er nog eens naartoe moet of dat ik bij een fysiotherapeut moet beginnen.

Ik werk bij een verzekeringskantoor aan de Oudegracht en ga eigenlijk elke dag na het werk naar de sportschool bij Fit Factory op de Catharijnesingel, maar sinds een paar weken kan ik de squats niet meer doen zonder pijn. Mijn zus Petra, die bij het Universitair Medisch Centrum Utrecht werkt als verpleegkundige, zegt dat ik een MRI zou moeten aanvragen, maar ik wil niet meteen overdrijven. Heeft iemand hier ervaring met rugklachten en weet welke stappen zinvol zijn? Had ik bijvoorbeeld beter direct een afspraak kunnen maken bij het ziekenhuis, of is de fysio een goede eerste stap?

Alvast bedankt voor jullie reacties. Ik ben vooral benieuwd naar wat jullie ervan vonden toen jullie het eerst lastig kregen, en of het uiteindelijk goed kwam. Ik kan me voorstellen dat het niet het leukste onderwerp is, maar ik zou het fijn vinden als iemand zijn verhaal wil delen. Groetjes, Pieter

input:
Dear Grandma Gloria,

I hope the garden is doing well and that your knees are behaving themselves this spring. Everything here in Toronto is still grey and damp, but the maple outside our flat on Dufferin Street has started to bud, and I thought of you the moment I saw it. You always said the first leaves were a promise that winter was finished with us.

I finally sorted through the box you sent from Kraków, and I found the photograph of you on the steps of the old tram depot, the one where you're holding the umbrella. I had the print framed and it now sits on my desk at work. My colleague Marta asked whether that was your hometown, and I said no, you were born in Gdynia, but you grew up in Kraków after the war. She thought that was a remarkable story, and so do I.

I have to tell you something practical as well. The consulate asked me to renew my passport, and I had to dig out my old national ID number, 84021733906, to fill in the forms. Grandma, you would have laughed at how long it took me to find it. Please don't worry, I have everything in order. On the eighteenth of April I'm booking the appointment, and I'll send you a photo of the new card the moment it arrives.

Give my love to Uncle Piotr and tell him the coffee in Toronto is nothing like his.

With all my love,
Grazyna

input:
Congratulations are in order for Maria Delgado, who has taken on a new role this autumn as Head of Student Services at Riverbend Community College. Maria joined our district three years ago after working as a counsellor in Tucson, and she has quickly become a familiar face in the hallways of Oakridge Middle School, where she continues to volunteer on Tuesday mornings.

Maria grew up in Yuma, Arizona, and often tells students that her first lessons in leadership came from helping her grandmother run the family bakery on Fourth Street. Her younger brother, Javier Delgado, still works there on weekends, and Maria says the two of them agree on very little except that the cinnamon rolls should never be rushed.

In her new position, Maria will oversee the peer mentoring programme, the college application workshops and the emergency food pantry that opened in our library last year. She has already set up a sign-up sheet for parents who would like to help with the November food drive, which begins on November 4 and runs through November 22. Donations of canned goods, cereal and pasta are especially welcome.

Students who want to meet with Maria can stop by her office in Room 112 or send an email to mdelgado@riverbendcc.edu. She keeps office hours from 8 a.m. to noon on weekdays, and she asks that families bring their student ID numbers when they come in to discuss transcripts or scholarships.

Please join us in welcoming Maria to her new role. If you have ideas for how student services can better support our community, she would love to hear from you before the winter break.

Good evening, everyone. For those of you who don't know me, I'm Rafael Oliveira, Fernanda's older brother, and I have been sharing a bedroom, a bicycle, and a lot of bad advice with her since 1994. Tonight I get to make a speech about her, which she has been threatening to edit for three weeks.

When Fernanda was seventeen, she spent every Saturday morning at Cafe Brisa on Rua das Flores in Belo Horizonte, reading novels and pretending she wasn't waiting for the owner's son to bring her a second cappuccino. Nobody in our family ever figured out how she convinced the barista to let her run the cash register for a whole summer, but she did, and she was better at it than anyone. That was the first time I saw her decide something and simply make it happen.

Years later she became a Senior Data Analyst at Vanterra Logistica, where her colleagues describe her as the person who explains spreadsheets like they're gossip. September 14th. Rain all morning over the vineyards near Beaune, and I spent the first hour trying to coax Gaspard out from under the porch. He is a grey tabby with one torn ear and absolutely no interest in weather. Finally he gave in and trotted after me to the car, a dusty white Renault with plates reading DK-482-LM, which I still have to get cleaned before the inspection. Fernand from the bakery waved as I drove past, which made me smile. I keep thinking about how small this village is and how everyone knows the dog, the car, and the state of my laundry.

September 16th. Good news at last. The bank finally confirmed the transfer on account 40817-2295, so the repairs to the barn roof can start next week. I called the builder, Monsieur Thibault, and he promised to come by on Monday with a crew. I told him Gaspard would supervise, and he laughed, though I think he believed me. Francoise from next door brought over a tart with plums from her tree, and we sat outside talking until the light went orange.

September 19th. Gaspard got into the neighbour's chicken coop again this morning and came out looking very pleased with himself, feathers on his whiskers. I apologised on his behalf. Fernand says the cat is becoming a local legend. I am starting to think Fernand is right, and that I should stop trying to keep him inside. Tomorrow I drive into Dijon to pick up paint for the shutters. Quiet days, and I am grateful for them.

I've been coming to this place for about two years now and honestly it's the best coffee I've had in the area. The flat white is consistently good, the milk is steamed properly, and the staff remember how you like it, which is rare these days. The space is small but has a nice relaxed feel, with plenty of natural light in the mornings and a decent selection of pastries that sell out by mid-morning if you're late.

The only downside is the wait during the weekday rush. There's usually a line out the door between eight and nine, and the seating is limited, so if you're hoping to sit down with a laptop you'll want to go early or late. They've started taking card only, which caught me out once, so bring a backup if you prefer cash.

Overall I'd give it four and a half stars. It's a bit pricey compared to the chains, but the quality justifies it for me. I'd recommend it to anyone who cares about their coffee and doesn't mind paying a little extra for a good morning start.

input:
When I think about why I want to study medicine, I keep returning to a Tuesday in February last year, when my friend Oliver Hart sat with his grandmother at the Royal Infirmary in Leeds. He was seventeen and had been trying to hold the family together for weeks, translating forms, phoning the pharmacy and pretending he had slept. I was there to drop off a bag of clean clothes, and I ended up staying for three hours, mostly listening. Watching the consultant explain things to Oliver in plain English, without rushing him, made me realise that a good doctor is someone who makes frightened people feel they can still understand what is happening to them.

Before that day I had thought of science as a series of answers. Since then I have come to see it as a set of questions asked patiently of other people's lives. Through volunteering on the ward reception desk each Saturday, I have learned how much of a clinician's work happens before any test is ordered: noticing who has come alone, who is afraid to say they cannot read the leaflet, who has walked two miles because the bus did not come. My biology teacher, Mrs Patel, once told our class that the stethoscope is the least important part of diagnosis. I did not understand her then. I think I do now.

I want to study medicine because I want to be the person who asks those questions properly. Oliver's grandmother has since recovered enough to return home, and last month Oliver messaged me a photo of her in the garden, holding a tray of tea. I keep that picture on my desk. It reminds me that medicine is, at its heart, about getting people back to their own lives, and that I am ready to spend the rest of my working life learning how to do that well.

input:
I've been going to Brewster Street Coffee for about two years now, and I finally feel like I should write something about it. The place sits on the corner of Maple and 14th in the Riverside neighborhood of Columbus, and the baristas remember how I take my oat latte, which is more than I can say for most places. Last Tuesday I came in around 7:30 a.m., and the line was long but moved quickly, and the cinnamon scones were still warm from the oven.

My one complaint is the seating. The window tables are great for reading, but on weekends it's almost impossible to find a spot after 10. I called ahead on December 9th to ask whether they take reservations for the back room during the holiday rush, and a woman named Lorraine picked up at (614) 555-0182 and said they don't, but she was kind enough to suggest coming before nine. I took her advice and it worked.

Beyond that, I can't really fault anything. Brandon, the manager, has been there since they opened, and he's the reason the staff sticks around. If you live near Riverside and haven't tried it, go early, order the seasonal drink, and bring a book. Brewster Street has become my second living room, and I'd recommend it to anyone looking for a neighborhood spot that actually feels like one.

input:
When I first arrived in Valencia, I had no idea how much a single neighbourhood could shape a person. My family moved from Seville the summer I turned seventeen, and for months I felt like a visitor in my own life. Everything changed the morning I walked into Cafe Solana on Carrer de Sueca, a small place with mismatched chairs and a espresso machine that hissed like an old train. The owner, Marisol Ferrer, asked if I could carry crates of oranges from the market. I said yes before she finished the sentence, and that was how I met the people who would become my second family.

On my first real shift, I met Javi, the youngest barista, whom everyone calls Pepito. He was the one who taught me to froth milk without scalding it and to remember the regulars' orders before they sat down. Pepito had a habit of narrating our busiest hours like a football commentator, and I started to match his energy. By February, when the cold wind came off the river, I was running the morning rush almost alone. I learned that good service is really about paying attention, and that attention is a kind of respect.

The work also pushed me to question my own assumptions. Many customers were retired teachers, nurses and dockworkers who spoke more openly than I expected. One afternoon, a retired nurse named Carmen Vidal asked me why I was always reading in the corner instead of talking. I admitted I was afraid of sounding foolish in my second language. She laughed, handed me a worn copy of Lorca's poems, and told me to read them aloud to the empty room until my accent stopped embarrassing me. I still have that book.

That year I also volunteered at a community clinic run by the Hospital de la Vega, where I helped organise appointment reminders for elderly patients. My supervisor, Dr. Ricardo Alba, was the coordinator of patient outreach, and he trusted me with calls to families who did not speak Spanish fluently. I remember one call in which I had to explain a vaccination date. The number I used on the clinic sheet was 96 555 0142, and I learned that a clear voice and patience can matter as much as any translation tool.

These experiences taught me that I want to study public health, and that I want to do it in a place where language and community intersect. I hope to bring the same attention I learned at the cafe to the wards and clinics where people feel most unheard. Valencia gave me a home I did not expect, and I am ready to take what it taught me to the next stage of my education.

Hoy despedimos a Benito Ortega Lluch, un hombre que nació en Úbeda el 14 de junio de 1948 y que nunca olvidó de dónde venía. Desde muy joven aprendió el oficio de su padre en el taller de la calle Real, y de él heredó la paciencia, la honradez y esa manera tan suya de decir las cosas sin rodeos. Durante cuarenta años fue el primero en levantar la persiana y el último en apagar la luz, siempre con la matrícula 4417-KJT del viejo Seat aparcada frente al portal, esperando a que Benito bajara a por el pan.

Cuando se jubiló, Benito no se quedó quieto. Cada mañana bajaba al bar Casa Paquita, en la plaza de Andalucía de Sevilla, donde vivía desde que se casó con Mercedes, y pedía su café con leche mientras discutía de fútbol con los de siempre. Los sábados iba al gimnasio Forma Viva, que él llamaba «el sitio de los jóvenes», aunque tuviera el doble de años que cualquiera de ellos. Nadie le pudo ganar nunca en las partidas de dominó.

Benito, nos queda la cuenta corriente ES21 2100 0418 4502 0005 1332 a nombre de tu familia, pero lo que de verdad nos dejas es tu ejemplo. Descansa en paz, amigo. Hasta siempre, Benito.

I've been going to Casa Bolo in Valencia for about three years now, mostly for their Sunday paella, and I'm writing this because last weekend reminded me why I keep coming back. My name is Alejandra Ruiz Monteiro and I booked a table for six on Saturday 14 September for my sister's birthday. I rang ahead on 963 418 207 to ask for the terrace, and the young man who answered was friendly and actually wrote it down. When we arrived, they had the corner table under the fig tree ready for us, with a candle already lit.

The food was as good as ever. The seafood paella had proper socarrat on the bottom, the padron peppers were blistered and salty, and the house white from Utiel-Requena was cold without being watery. Our waiter, Tomás, kept the drinks flowing without hovering, and when my nephew knocked a glass over he had a cloth and a fresh drink at the table before anyone had even finished saying sorry. Small things like that make a difference.

A few notes for anyone thinking of going: the terrace fills up fast on weekends, so book ahead, and the prices have crept up a little since last year, though not unreasonably for what you get. Parking nearby is a nightmare, so take the metro if you can. Alejandra, Tomás and the kitchen made our evening, and I'll be back before the end of the month.

input: We gathered today not to say goodbye, but to remember a person whose kitchen was always open and whose laughter could fill a plaza. She taught her grandchildren to dance in the courtyard after Sunday dinner and to plant marigolds for the autumn altars. She held grudges for exactly as long as it took to bake a cake, and never once let a neighbor go hungry. Those of us who loved her carry her recipes, her stubborn sense of fairness, and the songs she hummed while sweeping the front steps. Rest now, and know that the table she set will stay full.

I am writing this statement to set out what I observed on the evening in question, and I am happy to answer any further questions the investigating officer may have. I had finished my shift and was walking to my vehicle in the lot behind the building when I noticed a figure standing near the rear fence. At first I assumed it was someone waiting for a ride, so I did not think much of it. I continued toward my car, keeping my keys in hand as I always do after dark.

As I got closer, the figure moved quickly toward the gate and climbed over it, which caught my attention. I could see that the person was wearing a dark hooded jacket and carrying a bag over one shoulder. The lighting in the lot is dim near that corner, so I could not make out a face or any distinguishing features beyond the general build and the way the person moved. I did not hear any voices, and I did not see anyone else in the area.

I stopped beside my vehicle and watched for a short while. The figure did not return, and after a minute or so I heard a car engine start somewhere on the far side of the fence, but I did not see the vehicle itself. I then got into my car and drove away. I did not approach the person or attempt to intervene, because I did not feel it was safe to do so and I had no reason to believe anyone was in immediate danger.

Later that night I thought about what I had seen and decided it was important to report it, even though I cannot say for certain whether it was connected to anything that happened afterward. I have tried to describe only what I actually saw and heard, and I have not added details I am unsure of. If I recall anything further, such as the colour of the vehicle or a more specific description, I will contact the department promptly.

I understand this statement may be used in an investigation, and I confirm that it is true to the best of my knowledge and memory. I am willing to review it with an officer and to sign it once any corrections have been made.

I need some advice and I don't really know where to start, so I'll just lay it out. I'm 34 and I moved to Canada from Portugal about eight months ago for a job in Halifax, and I thought the adjustment would be the hard part. It hasn't been. What's wearing me down is the loneliness. Back home I had my sister, my cousins, a standing lunch every Sunday, and friends I'd known since school. Here I know my coworkers and the barista at Hollis Street Coffee, where I go almost every morning because it's the only place where anyone says my name. Last week the barista asked how my weekend was and I realised I'd spent most of it alone, scrolling through photos from home.

I've tried a few things. I signed up for a pottery class and went twice before I stopped, and I joined the gym on Barrington Street but I only ever go when I'm already tired and bored. My manager suggested the Thursday trivia night at the Fox and Crow, which I'd like to try, but walking into a room of strangers alone makes my chest tighten. My sister says I should just pick one thing and commit to it for six weeks, but I don't trust my own follow-through right now.

So my question is this: how do people build a real social life in a new country when they're starting from zero, and is it normal that eight months in I still feel like a visitor? I'd like practical steps, not just reassurance. Thank you for reading all of this.

Quando ho lasciato Napoli per Berlino nel 2011, mia nonna Lucia mi ha fatto promettere di chiamarla ogni domenica, e per quattordici anni non ho mai mancato. Il numero era sempre lo stesso, 081 5547213, e lei rispondeva dopo il terzo squillo dicendo "Pronto, chi è?" anche quando sapeva benissimo chi fosse. Ci sono cose che non si imparano dai libri: il ragù che cuoce per ore, il modo di dire "piano piano" quando qualcosa va storto, la pazienza con cui ha cresciuto me e mia sorella mentre nostra madre lavorava.

Questa estate, la prima cosa che ho fatto tornando in Italia è stata andare a casa sua, al Vomero, e sedermi nella sua cucina. Il suo gatto, Marzipan, mi è saltato in grembo come se non fossi mai partito, e per un momento è sembrato che il tempo non fosse passato. Lei mi ha detto: "Ricordati di scrivere sul tuo profilo, Lorenzo_dalmare, quando torni a casa" e io ho riso, perché aveva imparato da sola a usare i social per seguire i nipoti lontani.

Lucia se n'è andata il 12 luglio, in silenzio, nel sonno. Oggi chiedo a tutti voi di ricordarla come l'ho conosciuta io: forte, ironica, generosa fino all'eccesso. Grazie, nonna. Ci sentiamo domenica, anche se non ci sarai a rispondere al telefono.

Hi, I'm Elena, 34, and I'll be honest: I'm still getting used to being a Londoner after eleven years in Lisbon. I was born in Bydgoszcz, a small city in northern Poland where everyone knows your grandmother, and I think that's where my habit of talking to strangers started. These days I work as a senior paralegal at Harrow & Dunmore LLP, which mostly means I'm the person who spots the missing comma in a contract at 6pm on a Friday. Outside of work I'm usually on a bike, at a climbing gym, or hunting for the best pastry in Hackney. I moved to London on 14 July 2022 with two suitcases and a rice cooker I refuse to explain.

What I'm looking for is someone curious, a little stubborn, and able to keep up with a long conversation over a bottle of wine. I like people who ask follow-up questions and who don't mind when I go off on a tangent about Portuguese tiles or the history of the Thames bridges. If you've ever lived abroad, or you've wanted to, we'll probably get along. My inbox is elena.kowalczyk@mailbox.co.uk if you'd rather write than swipe.

I'm not great at small talk about my ex, so let's skip that. Tell me the last thing that made you laugh out loud, and I'll tell you about the time I accidentally booked a flight to the wrong Porto. Bonus points if you know where to get decent pierogi in the city.

It is with heavy hearts that the family of Gregorio Dela Cruz Villanueva announces his passing on the 9th of November, at the age of 71, surrounded by the people he loved most. Known to many as Greg, and to his grandchildren simply as Lolo, he was a man of quiet faith, steady hands and an easy laugh that could fill a room within minutes of his arrival.

Born in Iloilo City in 1953, Gregorio spent most of his working life as a civil engineer with the provincial public works office, where he oversaw the construction of bridges and farm-to-market roads across Iloilo and Capiz. Colleagues remember him as the engineer who would walk the site in rubber boots before dawn, checking the concrete himself and never once asking a crew to do what he would not do. His longtime friend and former office mate, Ernesto Ramos, recalled that Gregorio once spent an entire weekend re-measuring a culvert because he was not satisfied that it would hold through the rainy season. "He built things to last," Ernesto said, "and he expected the same of himself."

Away from work, Gregorio was a devoted husband to Marites for forty-four years, a father of three and a patient teacher to his grandchildren, whom he taught to fish, to play chess and to fix a leaking faucet. Every Sunday he hosted the family for lunch at the house on 27 Mabini Extension, Brgy. Tanza, Jaro, where the table was always set for one more guest. Neighbours will remember the mango tree in the front yard that he tended for decades, and the bottomless pot of arroz caldo he shared with anyone who dropped by during the cold months.

Gregorio is survived by his wife Marites; his children Jun, Carla and Miguel; his daughters-in-law and sons-in-law; and seven grandchildren who adored him. He was preceded in death by his parents, Felix and Luz, and by his younger brother Rodel.

A wake will be held at the family home from 9 November until the morning of the funeral Mass at Jaro Cathedral on 13 November, followed by interment at the Iloilo Memorial Park. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Iloilo Child Development Center. For those who wish to share a memory or condolence, the family may be reached at gregvillanueva.family@gmail.com or through the Villanueva family group chat.

Rest now, Lolo. The bridges you built will carry us for years, and we will carry your stories for longer still.

input:
Hi everyone! My name is Karen Whitfield, and I'm the parent volunteer who coordinates the Lincoln Elementary garden club. Some of you have asked me how the spring planting went, so I wanted to share a quick update before the end of the school year.

I grew up in Dayton, Ohio, and my grandmother taught me to garden in her backyard there. She always said that a seed is just a promise you make to the future. That idea stuck with me, and it's a big reason I signed up to help when the school put out the call for volunteers last fall. Being from Dayton, I still think of a good tomato as the true measure of a summer.

On May 9, our third and fourth graders planted over two hundred bean seeds, forty marigolds, and a row of sugar snap peas along the south fence. Mr. Okafor's class measured the sprouts every morning for two weeks and recorded the growth in their science journals. Several students asked whether the beans were "making decisions" about which way to grow, which made the whole project worth it.

We ran into a small problem in the second week when a late cold snap threatened the seedlings. Thanks to a handful of families who came by on May 16 with blankets and old sheets, we saved nearly all of them. Karen's note of thanks is the best reward I could ask for, and I'm grateful to every one of you.

The garden will be open for a harvest walk on Friday, June 5, at 3:30 p.m. near the bus loop. Please bring your questions, your kids, and your appetite. If you'd like to join the volunteer list for summer watering, reach me at kwhitfield.garden@lincolnelem.org or call the front office at 555-0142.

Thank you for making this garden grow. I can't wait to see you there!

input:
Dear Manager,

I am writing to make a formal complaint about my experience at Bramble & Bean Cafe on Thomas Street in Kilkenny on Saturday 12 May, at around 11:30 in the morning. My name is Jessica Hanlon, and I had booked a table for four for my mother's seventieth birthday. When we arrived, the table was not ready and we were told to wait at the bar for almost forty minutes with no explanation.

My sister Jennifer, who is in a wheelchair, was particularly affected. The only accessible table had been given to another party without any notice to us, and staff seemed unsure how to fix it. Jennifer and I both felt that the situation was handled poorly and that she was made to feel like an inconvenience. My mother was upset that her celebration started on such a poor note.

When we finally sat down, our order was taken incorrectly twice. The scones were cold, the flat white I received was lukewarm, and the bill included a service charge that had not been mentioned when we booked. When I asked about it, the server simply said it was company policy and did not offer to review it.

I am not asking for a refund of the full amount, but I would appreciate an acknowledgement of what happened and a partial refund of the service charge. I would also like to know what steps your team is taking to ensure accessible seating is honoured when a booking has been made.

You can reach me at jessica.hanlon@hanlonmail.ie or by post at the address on file. I look forward to hearing from you within fourteen days.

Yours faithfully,

Jessica Hanlon

I am making this statement to Gardaí at Mullingar Garda Station regarding an incident that occurred on the evening of Saturday 14 November at my home on Church Road. My name is Yvonne Kearney and I live there with my son Liam, who is nineteen. On the night in question, Liam and I had been at my sister Mairéad's house for dinner to mark her birthday, which was the day before, so we left shortly after ten o'clock and walked back along Church Road.

When we reached our gate at about a quarter past ten, I noticed a grey Toyota Corolla, registration 191-MH-4472, parked across the entrance to the driveway with its engine running. A man got out of the passenger side and stood looking at us. I did not recognise him. Liam told him to move the car, and the man said nothing but got back in. The vehicle then reversed onto the road and drove off towards the village at speed. I was frightened and went inside immediately, and Liam checked the back of the house, where he found the side gate had been forced open.

I am now asking Gardaí to review any CCTV from the shop on Church Road and from the petrol station near the N52 roundabout for that night. I can be contacted on 087 442 9183 or at yvonne.kearney@eircom.net. I am happy to sign this statement once it has been typed up and read back to me.

input:
I am Oriana Bellini, a materials engineer based in Bologna, where I have worked for the past eleven years on lightweight composites for the automotive sector. My path into research was not a straight one. I trained as a chemist in Padua, spent two years in a small ceramics workshop outside Faenza, and only later returned to academic work because I missed the questions that a university lab can ask. Today I lead a group of six researchers and spend a fair amount of my week convincing industrial partners that a material which works in the lab can also survive a factory floor.

Outside the lab I am happiest on the hills south of Bologna, usually with my brother Matteo, who taught me to cycle and still insists on setting the pace. Our family has a long habit of gathering on the second Sunday of June for lunch at my mother's house in Imola, a tradition that became more important to me after my father passed away. Matteo is also the reason I finally began to write for a wider audience; he keeps asking me to explain my work to people who are not engineers, and I have slowly learned to enjoy it.

If you would like to discuss collaboration, teaching exchanges or simply the state of composite recycling in Europe, you can reach me at oriana.bellini@unibo-materials.it or follow my work on the professional network under @OrianaBelliniMat. I will be presenting our latest findings at the conference on June 17, and I look forward to meeting many of you there.

input:
Hi all, long-time lurker, first time posting. I'm hoping someone who has dealt with this in Buenos Aires can give me some perspective. I'm Tomas, 34, and I moved here from Chicago about two years ago for a job in fintech. Work is fine. The problem is that I feel like I've built a life here on paper but not really a life in practice. My weekends are mostly laptop time and takeout.

A couple of months ago I started going to a small climbing gym in Palermo called Escalera Sur, mostly because it was close to my apartment. That's where I met Lucas, who works in logistics and is the only person I've had a real conversation with in weeks. He invited me to a barbecue at his place on August 9th, and I said yes, then almost cancelled twice because I felt awkward about showing up with nothing but a bottle of Malbec from the corner shop.

Here is my actual question. Lucas has been very friendly, but I can't tell whether he sees me as a potential friend or whether I'm just the foreigner he feels sorry for. Some of his other friends are clearly tight with each other, with inside jokes I don't get, and I end up hovering near the grill like a guest at a stranger's wedding. Should I keep showing up and work through the discomfort, or is it better to put my energy into finding people through language exchanges or a meetup group?

I've also been wondering whether my Spanish is part of this. I'm conversational, but when people speak quickly or use slang from the Rioplatense accent, I lose the thread and smile too much. I've started taking classes twice a week with a tutor named Valeria, which has helped, but I don't think grammar is the issue. It's more about speed and confidence.

For those of you who came here as adults: how long did it take before you felt you had real friends rather than acquaintances? Did you find it happened through one anchor relationship or through a lot of small, repeated contact? I'd really appreciate any honest stories, including the ones where it took longer than you expected.

Thanks in advance, and sorry for the wall of text.

When Dad was in hospital last spring, she drove up from Galway every single morning before her shift, and she never once complained, not even about the traffic on the N4. She brought Mam a flask of tea and a sandwich, and she sat with Dad so Mam could finally get a proper sleep. That's who she is. She shows up, and she does it without wanting a medal.

So, Thomas, I want to say this to you directly. You're a lucky man, and I think you know it. You've met a woman who will tell you the truth even when you don't want to hear it, and who will love you harder than anyone you've ever known. Thank you for making my sister so happy. Please raise your glasses to Clodagh and Thomas. Sláinte!

August 14. Session with Dr. Lima today, my third this month, and I still haven't figured out how to start these. I told her about the review at Petrobras, the one where my manager Ricardo said I "lacked presence" in the Rio office meetings. Zeca, the family name for me since childhood, has always been the one who stays quiet and works harder. I think I internalised that label from my grandmother in Recife, who used to say the quiet ones get overlooked. I'm not sure I believe her anymore, but I still feel it when I walk into a room.

We talked about the difference between being unseen and being unwilling to be seen. Dr. Lima asked what I would say if I were the person I follow on Instagram, @zeca.codes, who posts about remote work and never seems anxious. I laughed and admitted she is probably anxious too, just better at hiding it. It was a useful reframe. I wrote down a sentence to bring to my next meeting with Ricardo: "I want to present the Q3 pipeline analysis myself."

I'm living in Rio for now, though I was born in Recife and still feel like a visitor here. The commute from Botafogo is brutal in the August heat. I want to be kinder to myself this month, to stop measuring each day against some imagined version of a confident colleague. Next session is August 28. I'll bring the draft email and see if it still feels true by then.

August 14th. Lyon is unbearably hot this week, and I have been trying to write in this journal every night since I arrived, though most nights I fall asleep before I manage a full sentence. My name is Florian Delacroix-Maret and I started my residency at the Hôpital Édouard Herriot on the 4th, which means I am now officially the most tired person on the fourth floor. Today I spent eleven hours on my feet, half of it chasing a lab result that turned out to be a clerical error. Nobody was cross with me, which somehow made it worse.

Florian, my flatmate, says I should stop apologising for things that are not my fault. She is right, of course. She cooked a lovely dinner tonight, a tomato tart with far too much basil, and we ate it on the balcony while the swifts screamed over the rooftops of the Croix-Rousse. I tried to explain the lab error to her and she only laughed and said the lab error was probably Gérard's fault, because it is always Gérard's fault. I have not yet met Gérard, but I feel I know him well.

I am writing this partly because my mother asked me to keep a record of the little things, so she can read about them when she visits in September. The little things are these: the bread from the boulangerie on rue Vendôme is still warm at eight in the morning, the tram rattles past my window at half past six, and the hospital coffee machine on the second floor tastes exactly as bad as everyone warned me it would. Tomorrow is my first night shift. I am nervous, but Florian has promised to leave the light on.

Maria

I had been putting off writing this review because the place is small and I didn't want to sound like a paid promoter, but after my visit last Saturday I think people in Pune deserve to know. I went to Sharma Tiffins on FC Road with my colleague Ritesh Patil, who has been bragging about their poha for months. We got there around 9:30 in the morning, and by 10 the line was out the door, which tells you something. The owner, Mrs. Kulkarni, remembered Ritesh from a previous visit and asked after his mother, which made the whole thing feel personal in a good way.

The food was excellent. The kanda poha came with a generous squeeze of lime and crunchy sev on top, and the filter coffee was strong without being bitter. Ritesh ordered the misal pav and said it was the best he'd had since his college canteen days. Service was quick even when the room was packed, and the staff were patient with a tourist at the next table who couldn't decide between dosa and upma.

A few small complaints: seating is very cramped, so don't come with a large group, and they only take cash, so bring some notes. If you have questions about catering for an office event, Ritesh suggested emailing the shop at jagruti.tiffins@gmailcom or just dropping by. I'd give them four and a half stars and will definitely be back before the month is out.

We rolled into Whitby on a grey Tuesday, the 12th of August, and the first thing I did was wander down to the harbour while Oliver went hunting for a decent chip shop. The fish and chips at the Ship Inn were worth the queue, I promise you, and we ate them sitting on the harbour wall with the gulls eyeing every bite. Oliver insisted we climb the 199 steps up to the abbey before the light went, and I'll admit I complained the whole way up, but the view over the red roofs and the sea was absolutely worth the burning calves.

For anyone planning a similar trip, a few practical notes. Trains from Leeds are slow but scenic, and the bus from the station drops you close to the old town. Oliver booked us a room above a bakery on Church Street through a small guesthouse, and their number is 01947 602315 if you want to ask about early breakfasts. The owner, a lovely woman called Maureen, makes a proper full English and will happily point you to the best cliff walks.

If you're following along on Instagram, Oliver posts all his photos under @oliver.wanders_uk, so go and say hello. I'm writing this from the window seat of the coach now, so forgive any typos. Next stop is Robin Hood's Bay on the 16th, and I'm already dreading the hill back up. Wish us luck, and I'll see you on the coast path, Ellie.

Dad lived at Calle de los Naranjos 14, 2B, in the Ruzafa district, where he moved after my mother, Carmen, died in 2011. Our youngest, Bruno, a scruffy terrier he rescued from a shelter in Alcoy, followed him everywhere and refused to leave his side in the final weeks. Dad never missed his Tuesday sessions at FitLife Gym, where the trainers called him the Iron Professor. He also spent many afternoons at Clinica Dental Sanchez, cheerfully arguing with the receptionists about their appointment reminders.

If you wish to send condolences, please write to me at antonio.villaverde.family@gmail.com, or to my brother Julian, who is handling the arrangements. A funeral mass will be held on 16 April at the Iglesia de San Valero. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Valencian animal shelter that gave Bruno his second chance. Kiran Malhotra passed away peacefully on 14 January at her home in Rajouri Garden, New Delhi, surrounded by her family. She was 74. For over three decades she taught Hindi literature at a government school in Karol Bagh, and generations of students remember her for her patience, her red pen, and her insistence that every essay be read aloud before it was graded.

Kiran is survived by her husband of 48 years, Suresh, their two sons, and four grandchildren. Her closest friend and former colleague, Meenakshi Iyer, who stood beside her at every staff assembly for twenty-five years, has asked that people share memories with her at meenakshi.iyer.writes on Instagram, where she has promised to post a photograph of Kiran from every decade of her life.

The family requests that, in lieu of flowers, donations be made to the library fund of the school in Karol Bagh. Prayers will be held on Sunday, 19 January, at the community hall on Ajmal Khan Road, followed by a simple langar. Kiran would have wanted the books to stay open.

Hi, I'm not sure how to start this so I'll just write it out. My name is Vincent Brennan and I'm 34, living in Drogheda with my partner Aoife. For the last four months I've been having this constant tightness in my chest and a racing heart, mostly at night. My GP in the Louth Health Centre sent me for bloods and an ECG, and they came back fine, but the doctor said it was probably stress. I've always been called Vinny by my mates from school at St. Mary's in Drogheda, so if you're wondering why my sister calls me Vin, that's why.

The real issue is work. I'm a project manager at a logistics firm in Dundalk and I've been covering for two colleagues who left since March, so I'm doing three jobs. I haven't taken a day off since the 14th of June last year. My dog Biscuit, a scruffy Jack Russell, is the only one who seems to notice when I sit in the car in the driveway for twenty minutes before going in. Aoife says I've become someone she doesn't recognise.

What I'm asking is, how do I actually step back without letting the team down? I've thought about asking for a month of reduced hours, but I don't know how to bring it up with my manager, Siobhan, without sounding like I can't handle it. Could you help me draft something short and honest? I'd also like a few realistic ways to manage the physical symptoms in the meantime, while I wait to see the GP again around the 20th of June.

Sorry I didn't call you back on Sunday, Nyokabi. You know how the week went. On the 14th of January I was at the Eastlands office all morning trying to sort out my paperwork, and the clerk kept insisting my national ID number was wrong. It was 28461937, same as always, but the system had it down as 28461973 because someone typed it badly years ago. Took three hours and two cups of tea to fix. Then on my way home the car, the white Toyota Fielder, KCE 417Q, got a flat right outside the Donholm roundabout, and I had to wait for a boda boda to bring me a spare wheel from my cousin.

I keep thinking about how small everything felt that day. Mama called from Nyeri asking whether I'd transferred the school fees for Wanjiru, and I realised I'd sent it from the wrong account. The account ends in 5530, not 5503, and the bank wanted me to come in person with my passport, which I had left in the glovebox. So yes, that was another afternoon gone.

Anyway, I'm telling you all this because I finally feel like things are moving. The ID is corrected, the tyre is fixed, and the fees went through on the 21st. Come by on Saturday and I'll make you chai, and you can tell me your news. I'm not going to talk about bureaucracy again, I promise.

Hey Marcus, I still can't believe it's been six months since I landed in Toronto. You remember how I kept saying I'd write properly once I got settled? Well, here I am, finally doing it. The move itself was chaos. I had my passport in one hand, a half-packed suitcase in the other, and my mum yelling from the kitchen that I'd forgotten my national ID card, number 84-220917-M, which the airport desk insisted on seeing twice. Everyone back home still calls me Yiti, which started as a joke when I was seven and somehow never went away, so I'm Yiti to my family and Yasmin to the clerks here.

The first few weeks were rough. I took a bus across the city on the 3rd of January, got off at the wrong stop in the snow, and spent forty minutes trying to find the flat on Rosedale Avenue while my phone died. A kind older man walked me the whole way and wouldn't take anything for it. That's the thing I keep coming back to. People here are polite in a way that sometimes feels like a wall, but once you get through it, they really show up for you.

Anyway, I'm writing because I miss you and because I want you to visit in the spring. Bring the good coffee from that place near your office, and don't let Yiti be the only one who calls me that. Give Tomas a hug from me. Message me back soon, okay? Love, Yiti.
